title: Munich court rules Suno's AI music generator infringed GEMA copyrights
subtitle: A German regional court ruled Suno unlawfully memorized and reproduced six protected songs, delivering the first substantive European verdict on generative-AI music training.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The Munich Regional Court ruled on July 31 that Suno, the US-based AI music generator, violated German copyright law by memorizing and reproducing six songs represented by GEMA, the German collection society for composers and publishers. The court ordered Suno to disclose the revenue it earned from outputs derived from the works and set damages to be quantified in follow-up proceedings. GEMA filed the case in January 2025 and argued that the model's outputs made unauthorized reproduction obvious. Suno said it disagrees with the ruling and is weighing an appeal.

The decision matters because it turns a widely repeated legal claim — that generative-audio models can produce near-copies of their training data — into a court finding, in a jurisdiction with a state-mandated licensing regime that AI companies cannot route around. GEMA CEO Tobias Holzmueller called it "a verdict of global significance," and it is the first substantive European ruling on whether AI music trainers must license the catalogues their models learn from, rather than a preliminary injunction or a settlement.

Suno's music-generation case has run in parallel with Boston litigation from the major US labels and with a separate GEMA action against OpenAI over lyrics. The Munich verdict lands into an ongoing debate about text-and-data-mining exceptions across the EU, where rightsholders argue that a machine that outputs recognizable copies of protected works cannot claim the exception. The pending EU AI Act general-purpose model rules, effective August 2, add a second layer — providers must publish a sufficiently detailed summary of training content, which weakens any "we can't tell what's in there" defense.

For learners: this is what a licensing precedent looks like when it forms — not a single dramatic statute, but a court finding of infringement in one jurisdiction that raises the price of ignoring rightsholders everywhere else. If you build with generative audio, the practical takeaway is to treat provenance and licensing as first-order product decisions, not a compliance afterthought. The models that survive the next 24 months will be the ones whose training set can be defended in court, not just described in a blog post.
